newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Angry PLO says Netanyahu killing peace process.
newsitem.headline: Angry PLO says Netanyahu killing peace process.

text.p: The Israeli government on Friday agreed to grant financial benefits to Jewish settlers in the West Bank, a move the PLO said was a decision to end the peace process.

The decision could entice more Israelis to settle in the occupied area and was a strong sign of defiance by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to world opposition to his plans to tighten Israel's hold on captured Arab land.
"It is a grave decision with grave consequences, it's a decision to end the peace process," said senior Palestinian peace negotiator Saeb Erekat.
The move came two days after Palestinian gunmen killed two settlers in a drive-by shooting near PLO-ruled Ramallah.
Erekat, speaking before Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's cabinet met to discuss the decision, told Reuters:

"To consider the West Bank as part of Israel and to expand and encourage settlements means Netanyahu is officially killing the peace process, which was based on the crucial principle of gradually ending occupation."
Under the landmark 1993 peace deal with the PLO, Israel's previous Labour government withdrew from much of the Gaza Strip and from most Palestinian towns in the West Bank.
But Netanyahu has pledged to bolster Jewish settlements, long seen by Arabs as a main obstacle to peace.

At its weekly meeting, Netanyahu's cabinet decided to reinstate benefits for West Bank settlers, such as lower taxes, that are already given to residents of so-called development towns inside Israel, to Israelis in Gaza and to those in the occupied Golan Heights.

"The rest of the communities in Judea and Samaria (the West Bank) will enjoy the benefits of "A"-level national priority area status," a cabinet communique said. The West Bank incentives were cancelled after Labour came to power in 1992.

Army radio said Finance Minister Dan Meridor, who on Monday had pushed through the cabinet a plan to cut state spending in 1997 by 6.1 billion shekels ($1.9 billion), demanded to know at Friday's session how it would pay for the benefits.
He received no immediate answer. The cabinet statement said the benefits would be implementated after a ministerial committee headed by Netanyahu works out the details.
More than 130,000 Jewish settlers live among nearly two million Arabs in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
"In practical terms, it does not add an additional house," government spokesman Moshe Fogel said about the incentive plan.
But a settlement drive under previous right-wing Likud leadership in the 1980s was fuelled in part by housing grants for Israelis who could not afford a red-roofed villa near Israel's major towns.
Arafat said on Thursday the addition of even one house to a settlement would be a violation of his peace deals with Israel.

A leader of a radical PLO group whose guerrillas carried out Wednesday's attck said Arafat's forces had begun a crackdown on the group, arresting scores of activists and barring a rally in the town of Ramallah.
Israel had demanded Arafat crack down on the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which claimed responsibility for the drive-by shooting near a settlement.

Since taking office in June, the Netanyahu government has given the go-ahead for the construction of thousands of homes in existing settlements but has yet to meet the demands of settler leaders to establish new outposts.
Settler leaders welcomed Friday's decision but said it did not go far enough.
"It is a Zionist answer but not enough of a Zionist answer," settler spokesman Aharon Domb said, demanding the government approve new settlements.
($1 = 3.28 shekels)
